topics.name: Characteristics and classification of living organisms

questions.q: Which is one of the seven characteristics of living things?
questions.why: MRS GREN: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition.

questions.q: In the binomial system, what are the two parts of a name?
questions.why: For example Homo sapiens: genus Homo, species sapiens.

questions.q: Which group has a body made of segments with jointed legs and an exoskeleton?
questions.why: Arthropods (insects, crustaceans, arachnids, myriapods) have jointed legs and an exoskeleton.

questions.q: Which structure is found in plant cells but not animal cells?
questions.why: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall (and often chloroplasts and a large vacuole).

questions.q: Where does aerobic respiration take place in a cell?
questions.why: Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration.

questions.q: An image is 50 mm long; magnification is ×500. What is the actual size?
questions.why: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 50 ÷ 500 = 0.1 mm.

questions.q: A group of similar cells working together is a…
questions.why: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism.

questions.q: Which of these cells contain chloroplasts?
o: Both root hair and palisade mesophyll cells
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some believed root hair cells have chloroplasts. They are underground and do not photosynthesise.

topics.name: Movement into and out of cells

questions.q: Osmosis is the movement of…
o: any molecules down a concentration gradient
water through a partially permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution
questions.why: Osmosis is the net movement of water from a higher to a lower water potential across a partially permeable membrane.

questions.q: Which process needs energy from respiration?
questions.why: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, using energy.

questions.q: A plant cell is put in concentrated salt solution. What happens?
o: It loses water and becomes plasmolysed
It gains water and becomes turgid
questions.why: Water leaves by osmosis; the cytoplasm pulls away from the cell wall.

questions.q: A dialysis tubing bag of sucrose solution is placed in water. The bag gets heavier. What has happened?
o: Net movement of sucrose out of the bag
Net movement of water into the bag by osmosis
Diffusion of sucrose into the water
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some thought sucrose moved out. Sucrose molecules are too large to pass through; water moves in by osmosis.

long.q: Define osmosis and explain why potato strips placed in a concentrated sugar solution lose mass.
scheme: B1: the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane
B1: the solution has a lower water potential than the potato cells
B1: so water leaves the cells by osmosis

questions.q: Which test detects starch?
questions.why: Iodine turns blue-black with starch.

questions.q: What are proteins made from?
questions.why: Proteins are chains of amino acids.

questions.q: Benedict's solution is heated with a sample and turns brick red. What is present?
questions.why: Reducing sugars give a green to brick-red colour with hot Benedict's.

questions.q: What is an enzyme?
o: A protein that acts as a biological catalyst
questions.why: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions without being used up.

questions.q: Why does an enzyme stop working at high temperatures?
o: Its active site changes shape (it is denatured)
questions.why: Heat breaks bonds holding its shape, so the substrate no longer fits the active site.

questions.q: What does amylase break down?
questions.why: Amylase digests starch into simple sugars (maltose).

questions.q: Which statement about enzymes is correct?
o: All enzymes work best at pH 7
Different enzymes have different optimum pH values
Enzymes are used up in reactions
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many believed all enzymes are most effective at pH 7; pepsin in the stomach works best near pH 2.

long.q: Explain why the activity of an enzyme falls when the temperature rises above its optimum.
scheme: B1: the shape of the active site changes
B1: so the substrate no longer fits / is no longer complementary, and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form

questions.q: What is the word equation for photosynthesis?
questions.why: Light energy, absorbed by chlorophyll, converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

questions.q: Which mineral ion is needed to make chlorophyll?
questions.why: Magnesium is part of the chlorophyll molecule; a lack causes yellow leaves.

questions.q: Gas exchange in a leaf happens mainly through…
questions.why: Stomata, opened and closed by guard cells, let gases in and out.

long.q: Write the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis and explain why increasing light intensity stops increasing the rate of photosynthesis above a certain point.
scheme: B1: e.g. carbon dioxide concentration or temperature

questions.q: Where is bile made?
questions.why: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

questions.q: What does bile do?
o: Emulsifies fats and neutralises stomach acid
questions.why: Bile breaks fat into small droplets (bigger surface area) and is alkaline.

questions.q: Where are most digested nutrients absorbed?
questions.why: The ileum has villi giving a huge surface area for absorption.

questions.q: Which disease is caused by a lack of vitamin C?
questions.why: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy; vitamin D deficiency causes rickets.

questions.q: What does xylem carry?
questions.why: Xylem transports water and mineral ions up from the roots.

questions.q: Which conditions increase the rate of transpiration?
questions.why: Higher temperature and wind speed and lower humidity all speed up water loss.

questions.q: Translocation in phloem moves…
questions.why: Phloem moves sucrose and amino acids from sources to sinks.

questions.q: Which tissue transports sucrose and amino acids in a plant?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many did not understand the functions of xylem (water and ions) and phloem (sucrose and amino acids).

questions.q: Which blood vessel carries blood away from the heart at high pressure?
questions.why: Arteries have thick, elastic walls to carry high-pressure blood from the heart.

questions.q: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood to the body?
questions.why: The left ventricle has the thickest wall and pumps blood round the whole body.

questions.q: What is the job of red blood cells?
questions.why: Haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in tissues.

questions.q: Why does the heart rate rise during exercise?
o: To supply muscles with more oxygen and glucose and remove carbon dioxide
questions.why: Working muscles respire faster and need faster delivery and removal.

questions.q: Which vessels carry blood away from the heart?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some thought veins take blood away from the heart. Arteries carry blood away; veins return it.

long.q: Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the wall of the right ventricle.
scheme: B1: the left ventricle pumps blood all around the body (the right only to the lungs)
B1: so it needs more muscle to create a higher pressure

questions.q: What is a pathogen?
questions.why: Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protoctists that cause disease.

questions.q: How does a vaccine protect you?
o: It makes your body produce antibodies and memory cells
It removes pathogens from the blood
questions.why: Harmless antigens trigger an immune response, leaving memory cells for a faster future response.

questions.q: Why don't antibiotics work against viral infections?
o: Viruses don't have the structures antibiotics target
Viruses are not living cells, so antibiotics kill them instantly
questions.why: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures (like cell walls) that viruses don't have.

questions.q: Where does gas exchange happen in the lungs?
questions.why: Alveoli have thin walls, a large surface area and a good blood supply.

questions.q: When you breathe in, the diaphragm…
questions.why: Contracting flattens it, increasing chest volume and drawing air in.

questions.q: Exhaled air contains more ___ than inhaled air.
questions.why: Exhaled air has about 4% CO₂ compared with about 0.04% in inhaled air.

questions.q: What is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
questions.why: Aerobic respiration releases energy from glucose using oxygen.

questions.q: What is made by anaerobic respiration in human muscles?
questions.why: Without enough oxygen, muscles make lactic acid, creating an oxygen debt.

questions.q: Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces…
questions.why: This is used in bread-making and brewing.

questions.q: Which is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some chose the photosynthesis equation, which is the reverse.

long.q: Describe anaerobic respiration in human muscles during vigorous exercise and explain why breathing stays fast after exercise ends.
scheme: B1: glucose is broken down to lactic acid without oxygen
B1: releasing much less energy than aerobic respiration
B1: afterwards extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid (oxygen debt)

questions.q: Which organ makes urea?
questions.why: The liver breaks down excess amino acids (deamination), forming urea.

questions.q: What do the kidneys remove from the blood?
questions.why: Kidneys filter blood and reabsorb what's useful, excreting urea, water and salts as urine.

questions.q: What is the correct order in a reflex arc?
o: Receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector
questions.why: Reflexes are fast, automatic responses through this pathway.

questions.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
questions.why: Insulin from the pancreas makes the liver store glucose as glycogen.

questions.q: In bright light, the pupil…
questions.why: Circular muscles of the iris contract, making the pupil smaller to protect the retina.

questions.q: A shoot bending towards light is called…
questions.why: Auxin collects on the shaded side, which grows more, bending the shoot to the light.

questions.q: What is a drug?
o: Any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
questions.why: This is the definition used in the syllabus; it includes medicines.

questions.q: Why should a course of antibiotics be finished?
o: To reduce the chance of resistant bacteria surviving
To make the next course stronger
questions.why: Stopping early lets the more resistant bacteria survive and multiply.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of sexual reproduction?
questions.why: Variation helps a population survive changes in the environment.

questions.q: Where does fertilisation usually happen in humans?
questions.why: The sperm meets the egg in the oviduct.

questions.q: Which part of a flower makes pollen?
questions.why: Pollen is made in the anthers, on the filaments of the stamens.

questions.q: Two heterozygous parents (Tt) are crossed. What fraction of offspring show the recessive phenotype?
questions.why: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt: one in four is tt.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are in a human gamete?
questions.why: Gametes are haploid: 23 chromosomes, half the body-cell number.

questions.q: What type of cell division makes gametes?
questions.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and gives genetic variation.

questions.q: Which sex chromosomes does a human male have?
questions.why: Males are XY and females XX.

long.q: In pea plants the allele for tall (T) is dominant to the allele for short (t). Two heterozygous tall plants are crossed. Use a genetic diagram to find the expected percentage of short offspring.
scheme: B1: gametes T and t from each parent
B1: offspring TT, Tt, Tt, tt

questions.q: Which is an example of continuous variation?
o: Eye colour in a simple cross
questions.why: Height has a range of values, influenced by genes and environment.

questions.q: What is the source of all new alleles?
questions.why: Mutation creates new alleles; meiosis and fertilisation shuffle existing ones.

questions.q: How do bacteria become resistant to antibiotics?
o: Resistant mutants survive and reproduce (natural selection)
Antibiotics change their DNA on purpose
questions.why: Antibiotics kill non-resistant bacteria; resistant ones survive and pass on the allele.

questions.q: In a food chain, what do the arrows show?
questions.why: Arrows point from the organism eaten to the one that eats it: the direction of energy flow.

questions.q: Why is energy lost at each trophic level?
o: It is used in respiration and lost as heat, movement and waste
questions.why: Only about 10% passes to the next level; the rest is used or lost.

questions.q: Which process returns carbon dioxide to the air?
questions.why: Respiration (and combustion and decomposition) release CO₂; photosynthesis removes it.

questions.q: What can happen when fertiliser runs into a lake?
o: Eutrophication: algae bloom, then decay uses up oxygen
questions.why: Excess nitrates cause algal growth; bacteria decomposing dead algae use up the oxygen.

questions.q: Why does deforestation increase carbon dioxide in the air?
o: Less photosynthesis, and burning or decay releases CO₂
questions.why: Fewer trees take in CO₂, and burned or rotting wood releases it.

questions.q: Which organism is used to make bread rise?
questions.why: Yeast respires anaerobically, releasing carbon dioxide that makes dough rise.

questions.q: In genetic modification of bacteria to make insulin, what is used to cut DNA?
questions.why: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences, leaving sticky ends; ligase joins the pieces.

questions.q: Why are bacteria useful in biotechnology?
o: They reproduce quickly and have plasmids that are easy to modify
questions.why: Fast reproduction and plasmids make them easy to grow and engineer.
